Meuschenia scaber, commonly known as the velvet leatherjacket, is a monacanthid fish occurring in temperate coastal waters. Newly hatched larvae, upon chorion rupture, emerge at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.000065 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000065 grams] based on extrapolations from egg dimensions of related filefish species. This lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its yolk reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that follows yolk absorption. Field surveys of adult populations indicate that the species attains an ultimate total length of 31 centimeters [Li = 31 centimeters], a value consistent with the maximum sizes reported for other temperate monacanthids. This maximum length, occasionally observed in large females, serves as a key reference point for estimating other life-history parameters and for comparing body size across the family.

Reproductive maturation in the velvet leatherjacket occurs at a well-defined size threshold. Sexual maturation, marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis in females, is reached at a total length of 18.99 centimeters [Lp = 18.99 centimeters]. Corresponding to this length at puberty, the wet weight at puberty for a fish of this size has been calculated as approximately 173 grams [Wwp = approximately 173 grams], a relationship derived from the species length-weight allometry. This reproductive activation represents a major ontogenetic shift, after which individuals are capable of contributing to the breeding population. The attainment of this size and mass is likely influenced by local environmental conditions, including food availability and water temperature, which may modulate the growth trajectory of immature individuals as they transition from the pre-reproductive juvenile stage to a reproductively viable adult.

The maximum recorded reproductive output of Meuschenia scaber has been estimated from the fecundity of the closely related species Stephanolepis hispidus, applying a scaling correction based on the difference in adult body mass. Under stable laboratory conditions maintained at a temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C], a gravid female with a total length of approximately 16.3 centimeters is estimated to produce, on average, roughly 712 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 712 eggs per spawning event] and approximately 1 spawning event per day [F_R_i = approximately 1 spawning event per day] as a maximum daily reproduction rate. This rate was derived from the expected annual fecundity of a similarly-sized individual and the number of days in a year. The reproductive activity of these spawning adults is likely concentrated during a defined seasonal window, with individual females capable of releasing multiple batches of eggs over the course of a single breeding season.

The maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, attained by Meuschenia scaber has been estimated from the species length-weight relationship. Based on the observed asymptotic length of 31 centimeters, the ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 740 grams [Wwi = approximately 740 grams] in the largest, presumably oldest, individuals. This value represents the culmination of a prolonged growth phase, after which somatic expansion slows considerably. In contrast, the average mass of a reproductively mature fish at the onset of puberty, at around 173 grams [Wwp = around 173 grams], highlights the substantial mass gain required between first maturity and the attainment of maximum body size. Such a trajectory suggests that post-pubertal growth remains significant, allowing individuals to increase their body mass by more than fourfold before reaching senescence.

Longevity records for the velvet leatherjacket, based on mark-recapture studies and age determination from otoliths, indicate a maximum lifespan of 6,205 days [am = 6,205 days] under natural conditions at a temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]. This estimate, equivalent to 17 years, was derived from individuals inhabiting waters at a stable temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C], a thermal regime that typifies the species core distribution. This extended lifespan, culminating in natural mortality through senescence, is notable among monacanthids and suggests a relatively slow life-history pace characterized by deferred reproduction and a substantial investment in somatic growth. Reaching a body length of 31 centimeters [Li = 31 centimeters] over such a prolonged period further underscores the species comparatively low growth rate, a trait that may render local populations vulnerable to overexploitation.
